usage: Standard polite call for help to anyone, strangers included
반말, shouted to a close friend or family member
Softer, more formal request when there's no immediate danger
누가 (someone) added when calling out to a crowd
examples: 도와주세요! 도와주세요!
Help! Help me!
Shouted twice — the bare cry that draws attention fast
가방을 못 들겠어요. 좀 도와주세요.
I can't lift this bag. Please help me.
Everyday non-emergency use; 좀 softens it to 'a little'
할머니가 쓰러지셨어요. 누가 좀 도와주세요!
My grandmother collapsed. Somebody please help!
Real crisis; 쓰러지셨어요 = honorific 'collapsed' for the elder
nuance: 도와주세요 is the all-purpose cry for help, built from 돕다 (to help) + 주세요 (please give/do for me), so it literally asks someone to 'do the helping for me'. In a true emergency you shout it bare and loud; for ordinary favors you cushion it with 좀 ('a little') or upgrade to 도와주시겠어요? to sound polite rather than panicked. The 반말 form 도와줘 is only for a close friend or younger family, never a stranger. The nearest alternative, 살려 주세요 ('save my life'), is reserved for life-or-death danger — use 도와주세요 for everything from a heavy suitcase to a medical scare. English speakers often say just 'help' as 도움 (the noun) or drop the 주세요 and bark 도와, which sounds like an order; keep 주세요 to stay both clear and polite.

mistakes: Saying 도움 to mean 'Help!'
도움 is the noun 'help/aid', not a cry. To call for help you need the verb plus 주세요: 도와주세요.
Shouting 도와 to a stranger.
Bare 도와 is a blunt 반말 command that sounds rude under stress. Add 주세요 (도와주세요) for anyone you don't know.
Building it as 도와 주세요 with the wrong stem, e.g. 돕아주세요.
돕다 is irregular: the ㅂ changes, giving 도와, not 돕아. The correct form is 도와주세요.

english: Save me! / Help, I'm in danger!
usage: 존댓말 cry used only in life-threatening danger
반말, screamed to anyone when there's no time for politeness
Set phrase shouted to a crowd; literally 'save a person'
Please, I'm begging you, save me
제발 (I beg you) added to plead for mercy
examples: 살려 주세요! 살려 주세요!
Save me! Help!
Bare scream when you fear for your life
물에 빠졌어요! 살려 주세요!
I'm drowning! Save me!
Context of mortal danger; 빠졌어요 = 'fell/sank into'
불이 났는데 못 나가요. 사람 살려!
There's a fire and I can't get out. Somebody help!
Trapped-in-fire scenario; 사람 살려 reaches a crowd
nuance: 살려 주세요 comes from 살리다 (to save a life, the causative of 살다 'to live') + 주세요, so it literally begs 'please keep me alive' — far stronger than 도와주세요. You use it only when your life is genuinely at risk: drowning, an attacker, a fire. The dividing line from 도와주세요 is mortal danger: a heavy bag gets 도와주세요, a person grabbing you gets 살려 주세요. Under such terror, politeness levels blur and even strangers may hear 살려 줘 or the fixed 사람 살려 ('save a person!'), which Koreans shout almost reflexively. English speakers mistranslate 'save me' as 저장해 주세요 (that's 'save a file') or reach for 구해 주세요, which works but sounds less desperate than the idiomatic 살려 주세요 / 사람 살려.

저장하다 means to save data/a file. To save a life you need 살리다: 살려 주세요.
Using 살려 주세요 for minor trouble like a heavy box.
It signals mortal danger and will alarm people. For ordinary help say 도와주세요.
Writing 살여 주세요 or 살려주새요.
The stem is 살리- → 살려, and the ending is 주세요 (not 주새요). Correct: 살려 주세요.

usage: The set alarm shout; same word to everyone regardless of age
존댓말 report of a fire to people around you
Fuller, clearer 존댓말 — good when phoning or reporting
저기 (over there) points to where the fire is
examples: 불이야! 불이야!
Fire! Fire!
Bare alarm cry that empties a building fast
불났어요! 빨리 나가세요!
There's a fire! Get out quickly!
Add 나가세요 ('get out') to direct people
주방에서 불이 났어요. 119에 신고해 주세요!
A fire started in the kitchen. Please call 119!
Real scene; 신고하다 = 'report (to authorities)'
nuance: 불이야! is the fixed Korean equivalent of yelling 'Fire!' — 불 (fire) + the exclamatory 이야, a 반말-rooted alarm everyone shouts no matter who's listening, because there's no time to be polite. To report rather than alarm, you switch to 불났어요 or the fuller 불이 났어요, which uses 나다 ('to break out'). The dividing line: 불이야! is the scream that warns a crowd; 불이 났어요 is what you say calmly to a 119 dispatcher. English speakers often try 불 알람! (mixing in 'alarm') or just say 불, but bare 불 only means 'fire/light' as a noun and won't read as an alarm — you must add 이야 (불이야!) or the verb 났어요 to signal that something is burning.

mistakes: Shouting just 불 to mean 'Fire!'
불 alone is the noun 'fire/light' and sounds incomplete as an alarm. Use the set cry 불이야! or 불났어요!
Saying 불 알람! for 'Fire!'
That mixes English 'alarm' and is not idiomatic. Koreans shout 불이야!
Writing 부리야 or 불이얌.
It's 불 + 이야 = 불이야!. Keep the ㄹ on 불 and the plain 이야 ending.

usage: I'm lost (lit. I lost the road)
존댓말, said to a passerby or staff when you can't find your way
반말 to a friend or on the phone with family
-어버리다 stresses it fully happened — more helpless
It's my first time here, so I don't really know the way
examples: 저… 길을 잃었어요.
Um… I'm lost.
Bare admission; 저… buys a beat to flag a stranger politely
친구 집을 찾고 있는데 길을 잃었어요.
I'm looking for my friend's house but I got lost.
Everyday context with 찾고 있는데 ('I'm looking for, but…')
지하철역에서 나왔는데 길을 잃었어요. 이 주소 어떻게 가요?
I came out of the subway station and got lost. How do I get to this address?
Real situation handing over an address to ask directions
nuance: 길을 잃었어요 literally says 'I lost the road' — 길 (road/way) + 을 (object marker) + 잃다 (to lose) in the past tense, which is exactly how Korean expresses being lost. Note the particle: it is 길을 잃다 with the object marker 을, not 길에 or 길이. To a stranger you use the 존댓말 잃었어요; to a friend, 잃었어. Adding -어버리다 (길을 잃어버렸어요) makes it sound more hopelessly done. The nearest alternative is simply asking 여기가 어디예요? ('where is this?'), but that only asks your location, whereas 길을 잃었어요 explains your whole predicament and invites help. English speakers say 나는 잃어버렸어요 ('I lost [something]') with no object, which leaves the listener wondering what you lost; you must keep 길을.

mistakes: Saying 나는 잃어버렸어요 with no object.
잃어버리다 needs an object. To mean 'I'm lost', say what was lost — the way: 길을 잃었어요.
Using the wrong particle: 길이 잃었어요 or 길에 잃었어요.
잃다 takes the object marker. It must be 길을 잃었어요.
Saying 길을 잊었어요.
잊다 is 'to forget'; 잃다 is 'to lose'. Being lost is 길을 잃었어요, not 잊었어요.

usage: 존댓말 to staff, police, or a passerby
반말 to a friend or family
분실하다, the formal/written word used at a lost-and-found or police desk
I think my wallet was stolen
도둑맞다 when you suspect theft, not just dropping it
examples: 지갑을 잃어버렸어요.
I lost my wallet.
Bare report; -어버렸어요 marks the loss as complete
택시에 지갑을 두고 내렸어요. 잃어버렸어요.
I left my wallet in the taxi and got off. I lost it.
Context with 두고 내리다 ('leave behind and get off')
여기 카페에서 지갑을 잃어버렸어요. 혹시 못 보셨어요?
I lost my wallet here at the café. Have you seen it by any chance?
Real scene; 혹시 = 'by any chance', softens the question
nuance: 지갑을 잃어버렸어요 = 지갑 (wallet) + 을 + 잃어버리다, where -어버리다 adds the nuance that the loss is total and you feel the regret, which is why Koreans almost always say 잃어버리다 rather than bare 잃다 for personal belongings. To a stranger or officer use 존댓말; with friends, 잃어버렸어. At an official counter you'll hear and may use the formal 분실하다 (지갑을 분실했어요). The dividing line: 잃어버리다 = you misplaced/dropped it (your fault or accident); 도둑맞다 / 도난당하다 = it was stolen by someone. English speakers calque 'I lost' as plain 잃었어요 (sounds clipped) or forget 지갑 takes 을, saying 지갑이 — but the thing lost is the object, so it must be 지갑을.

The wallet is the object of 잃어버리다, so use 을: 지갑을 잃어버렸어요.
Saying 지갑을 잃어버렸어요 when it was clearly stolen.
잃어버리다 implies you misplaced it. If stolen, say 지갑을 도둑맞았어요 or 도난당했어요.
Confusing 지갑 with 가방.
지갑 is a wallet/purse; 가방 is a bag. Name the right item: 지갑을 잃어버렸어요.

usage: 존댓말 to police, embassy, or hotel staff
반말 to a friend or family member
분실하다 at a police station or embassy desk
I need to get my passport reissued
재발급 받다, the natural next step you mention
examples: 여권을 잃어버렸어요.
I lost my passport.
Bare report at a counter; -어버렸어요 = it's fully gone
호텔에서 여권을 잃어버렸어요. 어떻게 해야 돼요?
I lost my passport at the hotel. What should I do?
Context plus 어떻게 해야 돼요? ('what should I do?')
여권을 잃어버려서 대사관에 가야 하는데, 경찰 신고부터 해야 하나요?
I lost my passport so I need to go to the embassy — should I report to the police first?
Real situation; 신고부터 = 'report first', asking the procedure
nuance: 여권을 잃어버렸어요 = 여권 (passport, a Sino-Korean word) + 을 + 잃어버리다. Because losing a passport is serious, you'll repeat it to several people — hotel staff, police, your embassy — always in 존댓말, and at official desks in the formal 여권을 분실했어요. The dividing line between 잃어버리다 and 도둑맞다 is the same as with a wallet: misplaced vs. stolen; for a passport, police will ask which, because a reissue (재발급) and a stolen-document report differ. The nearest follow-up phrase is 여권 재발급 받아야 해요 ('I need it reissued'). English speakers mispronounce 여권 as 여건 (a different word, 'conditions') or drop the 을; keep the crisp 여권 and the object marker: 여권을 잃어버렸어요.

mistakes: Saying 여건을 잃어버렸어요.
여건 means 'circumstances/conditions'. A passport is 여권: 여권을 잃어버렸어요.
Dropping the object marker: 여권 잃어버렸어요 in a formal report.
In casual speech 을 can drop, but for a clear official report keep it: 여권을 잃어버렸어요.
Using 잃어버렸어요 when it was stolen.
If stolen, the police need 여권을 도둑맞았어요 / 도난당했어요, which triggers a different report.

usage: 존댓말 request to a bystander or staff
반말 to a friend in a sudden crisis
Could you please call the police?
More formal/polite when slightly less urgent
112 is Korea's police number; 신고하다 = 'report a crime'
examples: 경찰을 불러 주세요!
Please call the police!
Bare urgent request to whoever is near
저 사람이 제 가방을 가져갔어요. 경찰 좀 불러 주세요.
That person took my bag. Please call the police.
Context with 가져가다 ('took/carried off'); 좀 softens
사고가 났어요. 다친 사람이 있어요. 경찰 좀 불러 주세요!
There's been an accident. Someone's hurt. Please call the police!
Real scene; 사고가 나다 = 'an accident happens'
nuance: 경찰을 불러 주세요 = 경찰 (police) + 을 + 부르다 (to call/summon) + 주세요. Note the verb: you 'call/summon' the police with 부르다, the same verb as calling a taxi or a person over — not 전화하다 (to phone), which you'd use for 112에 전화해 주세요. To a stranger use 존댓말; in panic to a friend, 경찰 불러 줘. The dividing line from 신고하다 is nuance: 부르다 = summon them to come here; 신고하다 = formally report the incident (경찰에 신고해 주세요 / 112에 신고). Korea's police line is 112 (fire/ambulance is 119) — mixing them up is the classic foreigner error. English speakers also say 경찰에게 전화 (to phone the police), which is fine but less natural in a shout than 경찰 좀 불러 주세요.

경찰 (police) + 을 + 부르다 (to call/summon) + 주세요.
English speakers also say 경찰에게 전화 (to phone the police), which is fine but less natural in a shout than 경찰 좀 불러 주세요.

mistakes: Calling 119 for police.
119 is fire and ambulance. Police is 112: 112에 신고해 주세요.
Using 경찰을 전화해 주세요.
전화하다 never takes 을/를. To phone the institution use 에 (경찰에 전화해 주세요 / 112에 전화); to summon them here, use 부르다: 경찰을 불러 주세요.
Saying 경찰을 불어 주세요.
The verb is 부르다 → 불러, not 불어 (which is 불다 'to blow'). Correct: 경찰을 불러 주세요.

usage: 존댓말 request to people around you; 좀 softens
반말 to a friend in an emergency
Could you please call an ambulance?
examples: 구급차 좀 불러 주세요!
Please call an ambulance!
Bare urgent cry to bystanders
할아버지가 갑자기 가슴이 아프대요. 구급차 좀 불러 주세요.
My grandfather says his chest suddenly hurts. Please call an ambulance.
Context; 아프대요 = reported 'he says it hurts'
여기 사람이 쓰러졌어요. 의식이 없어요. 빨리 구급차 좀 불러 주세요!
Someone collapsed here. They're unconscious. Quickly, call an ambulance!
Real scene; 의식이 없다 = 'is unconscious'
nuance: 구급차 좀 불러 주세요 = 구급차 (ambulance, lit. 'emergency-relief car') + 좀 ('a little/please') + 부르다 + 주세요. As with the police, you 'summon' an ambulance with 부르다, not 전화하다; but since you dial 119 yourself or ask someone to, you'll also hear 119에 전화해 주세요. The 좀 here isn't really 'a little' — it's a softener that makes the urgent request sound natural rather than barked. The dividing line: 구급차 불러 주세요 = get an ambulance to come; 응급실 = the ER room you go to. Remember the number is 119 (not 911 as in the US, not 112 which is police). English speakers say 앰뷸런스 (the loanword) — understood, but the native 구급차 is clearer to a Korean dispatcher and bystanders.

Using 구급차를 전화해 주세요.
To summon it, use 부르다: 구급차 좀 불러 주세요. To phone the number, say 119에 전화해 주세요.
Confusing 구급차 (ambulance) with 구급상자 (first-aid kit).
구급상자 is a first-aid box. You need the vehicle: 구급차 좀 불러 주세요.

usage: 존댓말 to a bystander; 119 = fire + ambulance
신고하다 stresses reporting an emergency, not just dialing
examples: 119에 전화해 주세요!
Please call 119!
Bare command to whoever has a phone
불이 났어요! 빨리 119에 전화해 주세요!

usage: 존댓말 reporting an injury to anyone
반말 to a friend or family
격식 -습니다, e.g. reporting to officials or 119
다친 사람 (an injured person) when pointing to someone else

I'm hurt.
Bare report; 저 ('I') makes clear it's you
넘어져서 무릎을 다쳤어요.
I fell and hurt my knee.
Context; 넘어지다 = 'fall down', 무릎을 다치다 = 'hurt one's knee'
계단에서 굴러서 발목을 다쳤어요. 걷기가 힘들어요.

Real scene; 발목 = ankle, 걷기가 힘들다 = 'hard to walk'

To name where, the body part takes 을/를: 무릎을 다쳤어요. Use 존댓말 to strangers and 119, 반말 to friends, and the crisp -습니다 when reporting formally. Marking the body part with 이/가: 무릎이 다쳤어요.

usage: The set alarm shout; same to everyone, no time for politeness
It's a thief! / There's a thief!
존댓말-flavored version when telling people calmly
저 사람 (that person) to point out the culprit
소매치기 specifically for pickpocketing in a crowd
examples: 도둑이야! 잡아 주세요!
Thief! Please catch him!
Bare alarm + 잡아 주세요 ('please catch him')
제 핸드폰을 가져갔어요. 도둑이야!
He took my phone. Thief!
Context; 가져가다 = 'took/carried off'
지하철에서 누가 제 지갑을 빼 갔어요. 소매치기야!

english: Where is this? / Where am I?
usage: 존댓말 to a passerby when you don't know where you are
Where exactly am I right now?
Spells out 'where I am' when really disoriented
examples: 저기요, 여기가 어디예요?
Excuse me, where is this?
Bare question; 저기요 flags a stranger first
택시에서 내렸는데 여기가 어디예요?
I got out of the taxi — where is this?
Context; 내리다 = 'get off/out'
휴대폰 배터리가 나갔어요. 여기가 어디예요? 이 근처에 지하철역 있어요?

Real scene; 배터리가 나가다 = 'battery dies'

usage: 존댓말, the standard way to flag your limited Korean
I do not speak Korean well
격식 -습니다, 한국말 is the more colloquial word for the language
examples: 죄송해요, 한국어를 잘 못해요.
Sorry, I'm not good at Korean.
Bare admission; 죄송해요 cushions it
한국어를 잘 못해요. 영어로 해도 돼요?
My Korean isn't good. Can I speak in English?
Context; -해도 돼요? = 'is it okay if…?'
한국어를 잘 못해요. 죄송한데 조금만 천천히 말씀해 주시겠어요?
I'm not good at Korean. Sorry, but could you speak just a little more slowly?
Real scene; 천천히 말씀하다 = honorific 'speak slowly'

The dividing line from 한국어 못해요 (without 잘) is degree: with 잘 it softens to 'not very good', without it sounds like 'I can't speak Korean at all'. The polite follow-up is 천천히 말씀해 주세요. English speakers say 한국어를 안 해요 ('I don't do Korean', sounds unwilling) or 한국어가 못해요 with the wrong particle — the language is the object, so 한국어를.

english: Is there anyone who speaks English?
usage: Is there anyone who speaks English?
존댓말, honorific 하시는/계세요 to a roomful of strangers
반말 to friends; plain 하는 사람 있어
영어 하실 수 있는 분 계신가요?
Is there someone who can speak English?
More formal/polite, e.g. at a counter
Asked of one person directly; 할 줄 알다 = 'know how to'
examples: 혹시 영어 하시는 분 계세요?
Is there by any chance anyone who speaks English?
Bare question; 혹시 ('by any chance') softens it
여기 영어 하시는 분 계세요? 도움이 필요해서요.
Is there anyone here who speaks English? I need some help.
Context; -서요 trails off to explain why
죄송한데, 영어 하시는 분 계세요? 제가 한국어를 잘 못해서요.
Sorry, is there anyone who speaks English? It's because my Korean isn't good.
Real scene; pairs with 한국어를 잘 못해서요
nuance: 영어 하시는 분 계세요? = 영어 (English) + 하시는 (honorific 'who does/speaks') + 분 (the honorific word for 'person') + 계세요 (honorific 'is there?'). Two honorific layers are at work: 분 (vs. plain 사람) and 계세요 (vs. plain 있어요), which is exactly right when you address a whole room of strangers respectfully. The dividing line from 영어 할 줄 아세요? is target: 계세요? scans a group ('is there someone…?'), while 할 줄 아세요? asks one specific person directly. The softener 혹시 ('by any chance') makes either gentler. Korean uses 하다 for languages: 영어 하시는 분, or 영어 할 줄 아세요? for one person.
Using 있으세요? wrongly here.
For 'is there a person', the honorific existence verb is 계세요 (people exist with 계시다): 영어 하시는 분 계세요?

usage: 존댓말 reporting an accident to 119 or bystanders
반말 to a friend or family
examples: 사고가 났어요!
There's been an accident!
Bare report; 가 marks 사고 as what happened
여기 교통사고가 났어요. 다친 사람이 있어요.
There's been a car accident here. Someone is hurt.
Context; pairs with 다친 사람이 있어요
고속도로에서 사고가 났어요. 차가 두 대 부딪혔어요. 119 좀 불러 주세요!
There's been an accident on the highway. Two cars collided. Please call 119!
Real scene; 부딪히다 = 'collide', 두 대 = 'two (vehicles)'
nuance: 사고가 났어요 = 사고 (accident) + 가 (subject marker) + 나다 ('to break out/occur') in the past. Korean says accidents and fires 'occur' with 나다, and the thing that occurs takes 가/이: 사고가 나다, 불이 나다. The dividing line: 사고 is any accident; 교통사고 specifies a traffic/car accident — give the specific word when phoning 119 so they send the right unit. The nearest report phrase is 사고를 당했어요 ('I had/suffered an accident'), which centers the victim, vs. 사고가 났어요, which simply states it happened. English speakers calque 'I made an accident' as 사고를 만들었어요 (wrong — accidents aren't 'made'), or use the object 사고를 with 나다; with 나다 the accident is the subject, so 사고가 났어요.

With 나다 the accident is the subject: 사고가 났어요. (Use 사고를 당했어요 if you want 'I had an accident'.)

Specify what kind for the right response: 교통사고가 났어요 for a car crash.

usage: 존댓말 to a doctor, pharmacist, or anyone
반말 to a friend or family
Name the body part + 가/이 + 아파요
examples: 저 아파요.
I'm sick.
Bare statement; 저 makes clear it's you
어제부터 머리가 너무 아파요.
My head has been killing me since yesterday.
Context; 어제부터 = 'since yesterday', 머리가 아프다 = 'have a headache'
배가 너무 아파요. 토할 것 같아요. 병원에 가야 할까요?
My stomach really hurts. I think I'll throw up. Should I go to the hospital?
Real scene; 토할 것 같다 = 'feel like vomiting'
nuance: 아파요 is the polite form of 아프다, which covers both 'to be in pain' and 'to be sick/ill' — one word does both jobs in Korean. The body part that hurts takes the subject marker 가/이: 배가 아파요, 머리가 아파요, 목이 아파요. The dividing line from 다쳤어요 is cause: 아프다 = pain or illness from any source (a cold, a stomachache); 다치다 = an injury from an accident (a fall, a cut). English speakers say 나는 아파요 fine, but then mark the body part with 을/를 (배를 아파요) — in Korean the body part is the subject of 아프다, so 배가 아파요. They also overuse 병 ('disease') to say 'I'm sick'; everyday 'I'm sick/unwell' is just 아파요.

structuredNuance.t: 아파요 is the polite form of 아프다, which covers both 'to be in pain' and 'to be sick/ill' — one word does both jobs in Korean. The body part that hurts takes the subject marker 가/이: 배가 아파요, 머리가 아파요, 목이 아파요. Everyday 'I'm sick/unwell' is just 아파요.
The dividing line from 다쳤어요 is cause: 아프다 = pain or illness from any source (a cold, a stomachache); 다치다 = an injury from an accident (a fall, a cut).
Note the irregular conjugation: 아프 + 아요 contracts to 아파요 (the ㅡ drops).
